  How the engine stores networks, chooses algorithms, and uses every core

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Speed matters when networks are large, when a measure is computed for
every network in a collection, and when a permutation test repeats a
computation thousands of times. In knappnet speed never comes at the cost
of accuracy: every algorithm is exact unless it says otherwise, and every
benchmark below is also a correctness check.

```{r}
library(knappnet)
```

## How the engine works

All computation happens in one engine written in Rust with no third-party
dependencies. R reaches it through a small C interface, which the planned
Python package will share, so a result validated once is validated for
every language. The R package carries its own copy of the engine's source
and builds offline.

### Compressed sparse rows

When a measure is first computed, R passes the engine only what it needs:
each edge's endpoints as integer positions in the node table and, if
relevant, the weights. Attributes never leave R. The engine stores the
network in compressed sparse row (CSR) form: each node's neighbors sit
next to each other in one array, sorted, with a second array marking
where each node's run begins. Directed networks also keep the reverse
layout for in-ties. Walking a node's neighbors is then a sequential read
of memory, which is what modern processors do fastest, and node positions
are 32-bit integers, so the structure stays compact. The structure is
built once per network and cached, so computing several measures does not
rebuild it.

Dense binary networks can also be held as bit matrices, where testing a
tie or intersecting two neighborhoods handles 64 nodes per machine word.

### The algorithm follows the weights

Whether a network is weighted, and what its weights mean, decides the
shortest-path algorithm, so the fastest exact method is always used:

| Network | Shortest paths | Cost per source |
|---|---|---|
| Binary, or all weights equal | breadth-first search | O(m) |
| Whole-number lengths up to 1024 | bucket queue (Dial 1969) | O(m + D) |
| Any other positive lengths | Dijkstra (1959), binary heap | O(m log n) |

Here m is the number of edges, n the number of nodes, and D the longest
shortest-path length. Whole-number lengths are added in exact integer
arithmetic. With real-valued lengths, two paths of equal length can sum to
slightly different floating-point values, which silently drops shortest
paths in some tools; the engine treats lengths within a relative
10<sup>-10</sup> as equal. Betweenness follows Brandes (2001).

The choice is automatic. A binary network never touches a weight array,
and a network whose weights are all equal is computed as if it were
binary, then scaled.

### Parallel work

Most measures repeat independent work for every node: one shortest-path
search per source, one neighborhood per node. The engine spreads that work
over all cores, using the operating system's threads rather than OpenMP,
which is unavailable on some platforms where R packages are built. The
`threads` argument limits it; `threads = 0`, the default, uses every core.

```{r}
karate <- as_netframe(igraph::make_graph("Zachary"))
all.equal(betweenness(karate, threads = 1), betweenness(karate, threads = 2))
```

### Reproducibility

Work is assigned to threads in a fixed pattern and partial results are
combined in a fixed order, so a computation repeated with the same number
of threads gives bit-for-bit the same result. Integer results (counts,
memberships, cliques) are identical for any number of threads.
Floating-point sums can differ in the last bits between different thread
counts, because floating-point addition is not associative; such
differences are far below every tolerance in the validation suite.

Randomized methods (Louvain communities and QAP permutations) use a
counter-based random number generator (Philox; Salmon et al. 2011). Every
task draws from its own stream, computed from the seed and the task's
number, so results depend only on the seed, not on which thread ran what
or on the platform:

```{r}
identical(cluster_louvain(karate, seed = 42), cluster_louvain(karate, seed = 42))
```

When no seed is given, one is drawn from R's random number generator, so
`set.seed()` works as usual.

## Benchmark results

The section below is reproduced from the project's README, which records
the latest published run.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
# Find the repository README by walking up from the article's directory.
find_readme <- function(dir = getwd()) {
  for (i in 1:6) {
    candidate <- file.path(dir, "README.md")
    if (file.exists(candidate) && dir.exists(file.path(dir, "crates"))) return(candidate)
    dir <- dirname(dir)
  }
  stop("The repository README was not found; build the site from a full checkout.",
       call. = FALSE)
}
lines <- readLines(find_readme(), encoding = "UTF-8", warn = FALSE)
start <- grep("^## Benchmarks\\s*$", lines)
end <- grep("^## ", lines)
end <- end[end > start][1]
if (length(start) != 1L || is.na(end)) {
  stop("The README has no single Benchmarks section.", call. = FALSE)
}
cat(lines[(start + 1L):(end - 1L)], sep = "\n")
```

Brandes, U. (2001). A faster algorithm for betweenness centrality.
*Journal of Mathematical Sociology*, 25(2), 163-177.
https://doi.org/10.1080/0022250X.2001.9990249

Dial, R. B. (1969). Algorithm 360: Shortest-path forest with topological
ordering. *Communications of the ACM*, 12(11), 632-633.
https://doi.org/10.1145/363269.363610

Dijkstra, E. W. (1959). A note on two problems in connexion with graphs.
*Numerische Mathematik*, 1, 269-271. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01386390

Salmon, J. K., Moraes, M. A., Dror, R. O., & Shaw, D. E. (2011). Parallel
random numbers: As easy as 1, 2, 3. In *Proceedings of the 2011
International Conference for High Performance Computing, Networking,
Storage and Analysis (SC '11)*. https://doi.org/10.1145/2063384.2063405
